**Claim 0: Home microwave ovens use waves at 2.45 gigahertz, about 2.45 billion cycles a second**
- EMF Portal: a frequency of 2.45 GHz is used for heating food in microwave ovens in homes. URL: https://www.emf-portal.org/en/cms/page/home/technology/radio-frequency/microwave-oven
- IEEE TechNav (Microwave ovens): most commonly 2.45 GHz. URL: https://technav.ieee.org/topic/microwave-ovens/
- Verdict: supported as written (2.45 GHz is 2.45 billion cycles per second).

**Claim 1: Microwaves penetrate only about 1 to 1.5 inches into food; deeper parts are cooked by conduction**
- USDA FSIS fact sheet 'Microwave Ovens and Food Safety' (archived): do microwaves cook from the inside out? No; microwaves penetrate about 1 to 1½ inches; in thicker pieces the center cooks by conduction of heat from the outer areas. URL: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/web/20120915114427/http:/www.fsis.usda.gov/PDF/Microwave_Ovens_and_Food_Safety.pdf
- University of Nebraska extension: the center of thicker food cooks by conduction. URL: https://extension.unl.edu/statewide/dodge/Know%20Ins%20and%20Outs%20of%20Microwaves%20for%20Safe%20Cooking.pdf
- Verdict: supported as written.

**Claim 2: The door mesh has holes much smaller than the 12 cm wavelength, so the waves cannot pass**
- The Straight Dope: at 2450 MHz the wavelength is about 12 cm and the door holes are about 1 to 2 mm across, so the mesh reflects the waves. URL: https://www.straightdope.com/21343269/what-keeps-microwave-radiation-from-leaking-out-the-oven-door
- Mental Floss: the mesh holes are too small for the microwaves to pass. URL: https://www.mentalfloss.com/science/physics/mesh-grate-microwave-purpose
- Verdict: supported as written.
